project.name: leap-coach
project.description: An AI-enhanced, avatar-led LMS for Students, Professionals, and Entrepreneurs, built around the coaching content of Prof. Vishal Gupta (IIM Ahmedabad). Pairs on-demand coaching topics with a LEAP AI tutor, auto-graded checkpoints, a per-topic credit system, live sessions, discussion, and a full admin CMS. Runs on an in-memory/localStorage mock until Clerk+Supabase keys are present, then auto-switches to real services.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: LEAP Coach is an AI-enhanced, avatar-led LMS built around Prof. Vishal Gupta's coaching content, serving Students, Professionals, and Entrepreneurs. The README lays out the full stack (Next.js 16 App Router, React 19, TypeScript, Clerk, Supabase, Razorpay, Gemini, Mux) and, critically, the project's defining trait: it runs entirely on an in-memory/localStorage mock until real Clerk and Supabase keys are supplied, then switches over automatically. Keep that mock-to-real switch in mind — it shapes almost every file you'll see in this tour.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: app/layout.tsx is the Next.js root layout every request passes through: it loads fonts, sets global SEO metadata and JSON-LD, applies a pre-paint theme script to avoid flash-of-wrong-theme, and mounts ThemeProvider around whichever auth bridge the app decides to use. globals.css supplies the Tailwind base and CSS-variable design tokens referenced everywhere else. This is the bird's-eye view of the runtime — everything downstream is reached through what this file mounts.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js App Router root layouts wrap every route in the app; a pre-paint inline script (set here before React hydrates) is the standard trick for applying a persisted theme without a visible flash.

tour.title: The Dual-Mode Auth Bridge
tour.description: This is the single most distinctive architectural decision in the codebase. lib/auth/types.ts defines a backend-agnostic AuthBridge interface; lib/clerk/config.ts holds one boolean flag (is a Clerk key present?) that decides which implementation app/layout.tsx mounts — the real lib/auth/ClerkAuthBridge.tsx (adapting Clerk's hooks for sign-in, OAuth, verification, password reset) or the inert lib/auth/MockAuthBridge.tsx (a no-op, since mock auth is handled directly by the store). proxy.ts is the root Next.js middleware that attaches the Clerk session to every server request when real auth is configured, or passes through harmlessly when it isn't. Nothing else in the app needs to know which mode is active — that's the point of the interface.
tour.languageLesson: This is the Strategy pattern applied to a whole auth provider: consumers depend only on the AuthBridge interface, and a single environment-driven flag swaps the concrete implementation at mount time — no conditional branches scattered through the UI.

tour.title: The Central Store: AppProvider
tour.description: Whichever auth bridge wins, it mounts lib/store/AppProvider.tsx — a single React context that holds every piece of domain data (users, courses, sessions, payments, notifications) and exposes every read/write action the UI calls through useApp(). AppProvider checks lib/supabase/config.ts's real-mode flag: if Supabase isn't configured it works entirely off lib/mock/seed.ts and localStorage; once configured, it fetches through lib/supabase/db.ts (row-to-domain mappers and CRUD helpers) using a session-aware client from lib/supabase/client.ts. This is why the product can be clicked through end-to-end before any backend is wired up — the store, not the UI, absorbs the difference.
tour.languageLesson: React Context as a mini state-management layer: one provider, one useApp() hook, and a single source of truth that hides a persistence-layer swap (localStorage vs. Postgres) behind identical action signatures.

tour.title: Core Domain Types and Utilities
tour.description: lib/types.ts is imported by more files than anything else in the codebase (67 dependents) — it defines the shared vocabulary (Course, User, Payment, Enrollment, and friends) that both the mock store and the Supabase mappers from Step 4 speak. lib/utils.ts is a close second (56 dependents), supplying the formatting and small pure helpers used across pages, API routes, and components alike. Understanding these two files means you can read almost any other file in the project without guessing at shapes.

tour.title: Marketing Site
tour.description: app/page.tsx is the public landing page — an async server component using ISR (revalidate every 600s) that server-fetches homepage content and pricing, then composes the Home* marketing sections. components/marketing/SiteNav.tsx is the public header, morphing from a transparent overlay into a floating pill on scroll, with auth-aware CTAs sourced from the same store built in Step 4. components/marketing/home/HomeHero.tsx shows the pattern used throughout marketing: render server-fetched content first, then swap in the live store once the client hydrates.

tour.title: Auth & Onboarding Flow
tour.description: Login and signup are client components that branch on the Clerk-configured flag from Step 3: app/login/page.tsx offers Google OAuth and email/password with a mock-mode fallback, while app/signup/page.tsx handles Clerk's 6-digit email-verification step or a direct mock account creation. After signup, app/select-role/page.tsx lets a new user pick student/professional/entrepreneur before routing to the dashboard. Both auth pages share components/auth/AuthShell.tsx (the two-panel branded layout) and components/auth/OAuthButtons.tsx, so the visual shell stays identical regardless of which backend mode is active.

tour.title: Authenticated App Shell & Lesson Player
tour.description: components/app/AppShell.tsx is the guard every logged-in route renders inside: it redirects signed-out, admin, or role-less users, then wraps the page in the shared header and container. app/dashboard/page.tsx aggregates a learner's world — enrolled-course progress, recommended topics, the next live session, a daily tip — into one home view. app/learn/[courseId]/[order]/page.tsx is the lesson player: it gates access by enrollment/unlock (using the entitlement rules you'll meet in Step 10), plays video, and hosts the AI tutor, notes, and discussion, while app/learn/.../assignment/[assignmentId]/page.tsx runs the auto-graded checkpoint quizzes.

tour.title: The LEAP AI Tutor
tour.description: components/learn/LeapChat.tsx is the in-lesson chat UI with quick actions (summarize/quiz/explain); it calls lib/mock/leapAI.ts — a mock responder grounded in the lesson transcript — as the explicit seam for the real Gemini call, echoing the dual-mode pattern from Steps 3-4 but scoped to one feature. On the server, app/api/leap/chat/route.ts authenticates the learner, rate-limits and bans abuse, builds a lesson-grounded system prompt, and proxies to lib/ai/gemini.ts (the single shared Gemini client with retries and safe-null-on-failure). app/api/leap/hint/route.ts uses the same client to generate a single non-revealing hint after a wrong checkpoint answer, escalating specificity by attempt number.
tour.languageLesson: Google Gemini is called server-side only — the API key never reaches the browser — and a 'safe null on failure' return convention lets the UI degrade gracefully to a local mock rather than throwing an error to the learner.

tour.title: Pricing & Checkout
tour.description: app/pricing/page.tsx is a server component that fetches live pricing (force-dynamic, no caching) so an admin-set price change shows correctly on first paint; it hands off to app/pricing/PricingClient.tsx for the interactive per-topic and category-bundle panels. components/CheckoutModal.tsx drives the full purchase flow — coupon validation, Razorpay script loading, and the order-create/verify round-trip — with demo-grant and local-only fallbacks when Razorpay isn't configured, once again mirroring the mock/real split you've now seen three times. lib/payments/server.ts is the authoritative pricing engine: it computes prices from the database, never trusts client-supplied amounts, and applies upgrade and coupon logic server-side.

tour.title: Razorpay Lifecycle & Access Gating
tour.description: A payment can complete in more than one way, so the app defends in depth: app/api/payments/razorpay/order/route.ts creates a server-priced order, app/api/payments/razorpay/verify/route.ts verifies the browser-side signature and fulfils it, and app/api/payments/razorpay/webhook/route.ts independently verifies and fulfils the same payment server-to-server — a safety net for buyers who close the tab before /verify runs. Both routes funnel into lib/payments/grant.ts, the shared idempotent fulfilment logic that grants entitlements and records the payment exactly once no matter which path triggered it. lib/access.ts then computes, from those grants, which category catalogs and courses a user actively holds and until when — the engine the lesson player in Step 8 checks before playing a video.
tour.languageLesson: Idempotent fulfilment is the key pattern here: because two independent code paths (browser verify and server webhook) can both try to grant the same payment, the shared grant function must be safe to call twice for the same payment id without double-granting.

tour.title: Admin CMS
tour.description: components/admin/AdminShell.tsx is the admin console's own guarded shell — permission-filtered sidebar navigation plus an auth redirect for non-admins, gating each section by owner/sub-admin permissions rather than a single all-or-nothing admin flag. app/admin/page.tsx is the command-center overview (KPIs, cohort breakdowns, recent purchases); app/admin/courses/page.tsx manages the published catalog, while app/admin/courses/new/page.tsx renders components/admin/CourseWizard.tsx — a multi-step authoring flow that converts between the store's Course model from Step 4 and an editable draft, uploading media to Supabase Storage as it goes.

tour.title: API Route Conventions
tour.description: Nearly every route you've seen since Step 9 leans on four small shared helpers: lib/api/validate.ts parses request bodies against Zod schemas and returns a generic error instead of throwing; lib/api/rate-limit.ts is a multi-tiered, in-memory sliding-window limiter with per-tier thresholds for AI, payment, admin, email, and Telegram traffic; lib/api/errors.ts enforces no information leakage by returning safe client-facing messages while logging full diagnostics server-side; and lib/api/banned.ts rejects calls from suspended accounts even if their Clerk session is still technically valid. Once you recognize these four, every API route in the project reads the same way.
tour.languageLesson: Zod schemas give runtime validation with inferred static types in one declaration — the same schema that rejects a malformed request body also produces the TypeScript type consumers use, so validation and typing never drift apart.

tour.title: The Database Schema
tour.description: supabase/database.sql is the complete, idempotent Postgres schema behind real mode: 37 tables with row-level-security policies keyed to the Clerk user id, plus the functions and triggers admin actions rely on. The payments table mirrors exactly the fields lib/payments/grant.ts writes in Step 11 (order/payment ids, status, grant status, refund fields); courses and enrollments back the catalog and progress logic from Step 8. supabase/README.md is the step-by-step guide for going live — running this schema, wiring Clerk to Supabase RLS, and configuring Razorpay webhooks — which is exactly the mock-to-real transition Step 1's README promised.
tour.languageLesson: Row-level security (RLS) pushes authorization into the database itself: a policy keyed to the Clerk user id means even a compromised client-side query can't read or write another user's rows, regardless of what the application code intended.

tour.title: Shared UI Primitives
tour.description: To close the loop, components/ui/Button.tsx, Card.tsx, Badge.tsx, and Field.tsx are the generic, domain-free building blocks that appear in nearly every screen you've toured — from the marketing site's CTAs to the admin CMS's forms. Button.tsx alone has 31 direct dependents, more than any other component in the project. They carry no business logic of their own, which is exactly why they could sit underneath the marketing site, the learner app, and the admin CMS without any of those layers needing to know about each other.
